titre: The Gulf Stream Chart the Post Office Ignored
accroche: In 1768, the British post office asks Benjamin Franklin why its packet boats arrive two weeks after ordinary merchant ships.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1768, the customs commissioners recently installed in Boston complain to the British Treasury: the official packet boats, sailing from Falmouth to New York, regularly take two weeks longer than ordinary merchant ships sailing from London to Rhode Island. Consulted on the question as deputy postmaster for the American colonies, Benjamin Franklin wonders: how can a slower merchant ship, which also has to work its way through the English Channel, arrive two weeks before a direct packet boat, when Boston and Newport are only a day's sail apart?

## A Secret Whalers Have Known for Generations

Franklin asks his cousin Timothy Folger, a whaling captain from the island of Nantucket who happens to be in London, about it. The answer is immediate: captains bound for Rhode Island know the Gulf Stream, those bound for Massachusetts do not. Nantucket lives off whaling, an industry that employs nearly 150 ships and keeps its crews constantly running along the edges of this powerful current, which flows out of the Gulf of Mexico, in pursuit of their prey. Having crossed it so often, the whalers know its course, its width and its speed better than anyone, up to four miles an hour at its narrowest point. They have even warned packet captains they found struggling against the current, which cost them as much as seventy miles a day. Franklin will later relate their answer: the captains “were too wise to be counselled by simple American fishermen.”

At Franklin's request, Folger draws the course, width and strength of the current on a chart, with directions for avoiding it. Franklin sends the whole thing to the secretary of the British post office, suggesting that it be engraved and printed for the use of captains.

## A Chart Printed, Distributed, and Set Aside

The chart appears in London around 1769, and copies are sent to Falmouth for the packet captains. They pay no attention to it. It is only in 1775 and 1776, on two personal crossings, that Franklin himself measures the water temperature, thermometer in hand, and confirms a difference of several degrees that betrays the current's presence. A third version of the chart appears in 1786 in Philadelphia, in a letter addressed to a French correspondent and published by the American Philosophical Society.

What this episode shows is therefore not the discovery of a current by a lone scholar, but the opposite: knowledge that was already old, accumulated over generations by sailors whom no one had thought to publish, put on a chart at the request of an administrator, then ignored by the very people it was meant for.

carte.punch: A whaling captain showed Franklin how to avoid a two-week delay, to no avail.
carte.idee: In 1768, Franklin discovers that the delay of the mail packets comes from the Gulf Stream: the Nantucket whalers, who cross it constantly while hunting, already know its course and speed. His chart is printed and distributed to the captains, who go on ignoring it.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The Benjamin Franklin and Timothy Folger charts of the Gulf Stream (Richardson, 1980)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The study by oceanographer Philip Richardson (WHOI), who tracked down the few surviving copies of the original chart.

quiz.question: Why did the Gulf Stream chart drawn by Folger for Franklin fail to shorten the British packet boats' crossings?
choix: Because the packet captains refused to follow its directions
Because the chart placed the current in the wrong spot
Because the current's course changed from one season to the next
Because the British navy banned its distribution
quiz.explication: Franklin had the chart printed and sent it to the British post office as early as 1769, but the packet captains, though warned by the whalers themselves, went on ignoring it: the course of the current was right, and it was those who could have avoided it who did not.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who first identifies the cause of the packet boats' delay, in 1768?
choix: An anonymous officer of the Royal Navy
Timothy Folger, Franklin's cousin and a Nantucket whaling captain
Franklin himself, through astronomical navigation calculations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Franklin asks his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain who happens to be in London, who answers at once: captains who know the Gulf Stream avoid it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Franklin personally confirm the presence of the current during his crossings of 1775 and 1776?
choix: By counting the difference in days between two different routes
By questioning sailors again on his arrival
By using a compass designed especially for the occasion
By measuring the water temperature himself, thermometer in hand
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is only in 1775 and 1776, on two personal crossings, that Franklin measures the water temperature and confirms a difference of several degrees that betrays the current's presence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What complaint triggers Franklin's inquiry in 1768?
choix: Rhode Island merchants denounce organized smuggling through Nantucket
The London press reports packet boats missing their postal deadlines
The customs commissioners in Boston complain to the British Treasury about the packet boats' delay
Whaling captains demand an exclusive postal contract
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The customs commissioners recently installed in Boston complain to the British Treasury that the official packet boats are late compared with ordinary merchant ships.
